transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, uh… what brings me here is my talking, mostly. It gets all mixed up, and I know it does because people keep stopping me or looking at me like I went left when I was supposed to go right.

Like I try to explain one thing—say, the keys, because the keys are important, you know, you need keys for doors and work and keeping things straight—and then somehow I’m talking about jail, and then I’m trying to explain the prayer rug, and then the chess pieces come in because that’s part of it too in my head, but when I say it out loud people tell me they can’t follow me. They say, “Slow down,” or “What are you talking about?” and I’m trying to slow down, but the pieces are all connected to me.

So I came in because I’m having trouble making people understand what I mean. It’s like the words are there, but they don’t line up right when they come out.
Can you describe what it feels like when your thoughts get mixed up while talking? Do the ideas feel connected to you even if others don’t follow them?

Yeah… yeah, they feel connected to me. That’s the part that’s frustrating, because inside my head it’s not random. It’s like there’s a line going from one thing to the next, but when I say it out loud, other people can’t see the line.

Like I start with the keys, because I’m trying to explain something simple, just the keys, and then the keys make me think of doors, and doors make me think of being locked in or jail, and then somehow I’m talking about the prayer rug because that’s connected too in my mind, and then the chess pieces come in, because it feels like moves and pieces and where things belong. To me it all belongs together, but I can see on people’s faces that they’re lost.

And then they stop me and say, “What are you talking about?” or “Slow down,” and I’m already trying to slow down, but the thoughts are kind of running ahead of my mouth. I know what I mean while I’m saying it, but then it comes out all tangled, and people tell me they can’t follow what I’m saying. That’s what brings me in, really. My talking gets all mixed up.
Have you ever experienced things that others don’t seem to see, hear, or understand, like hearing voices or believing something strongly that others say isn’t true?

Yeah… I mean, yes. I don’t always like saying it that way because it makes it sound like I’m trying to be strange, but sometimes I hear this man’s voice. Not like a thought exactly, not like when you remember somebody talking. It sounds like it’s coming from outside me.

A lot of times it’s from the vents, like in the building, or near the mop closet. I’ll be cleaning and then I hear my name, clear enough that I turn around because I think somebody’s there. And then there isn’t anybody there. Sometimes it says I ruined everything. Just that kind of thing, like accusing me. And it sounds real, like a person standing right beside me, not quiet in the back of my head.

I’ll check the hallway, or I’ll open the closet, because I’m thinking maybe someone’s messing with me or hiding there, but then there’s nobody. And then I feel embarrassed because I’m standing there with the mop or the keys and I’m trying to figure out if I heard it or if other people heard it too. Usually nobody else seems to notice.
Have there been times when you believed something very strongly that others told you wasn’t true, even though it made sense to you at the time?

Yeah… yes, that has happened. I know it sounds bad when I say it straight, but at the time it didn’t feel like I was making it up. It felt obvious, like if you were standing where I was standing you’d see it too.

There was this thing at the building where I was sure the building people had marked me somehow. Not like with paint or something you could point to, but marked me as in they all knew something about me, and they were passing it around without saying it straight. The hallway lights would flicker or come on at certain times, and then somebody would give me a little look, just a quick look, and to me it meant they were warning each other about me. Like, “There he is,” or “Watch him.” It made sense to me because the lights, the timing, the looks, the way people got quiet when I came around — it all lined up in my head.

My supervisor tried to show me on the camera that nothing was happening. He pulled it up and said, “See, nobody’s doing anything, nobody’s signaling.” And I could see what he was showing me, I really could, but it didn’t settle it for me. I still felt sure there was something underneath it, like the camera just wasn’t catching the real part, or they knew where the cameras were. Even with him saying it wasn’t true, I couldn’t shake it. It still felt like the building people had me marked and were using the lights and those little looks to warn each other.
Have there been times when you felt down, hopeless, or lost interest in things for several days in a row, to the point where it was hard to get through the day?

Yeah… yes, that happens. More than I like to admit, honestly. There are days where I wake up and it’s like something is already sitting on my chest before I even stand up. I’ll do morning prayer, or try to, and then afterward I just sit on the edge of the bed for a long time.

I’m not even doing anything. Just sitting there. And I feel heavy, like my arms and legs are full of wet sand or something. Empty at the same time, if that makes sense. Heavy and empty together. I’ll look at my clothes, or think about washing up, brushing my teeth, getting myself together, and it feels like… what’s the point? Like going outside would take more out of me than I have.

It’s not just being tired from work. It’s more like I can’t find a reason to start. Cleaning myself up, stepping out the door, doing regular things—on those bad days it all feels too far away. I just sit there and the day starts passing without me.

Have you ever experienced other things that others don’t seem to notice, like seeing things that aren’t there or believing something strongly that others say isn’t true, outside of what you’ve already described?

I’m not sure there’s more than what I already said. I mean… the voice and the thing with the lights and people looking at me, that’s the main stuff I know how to explain.

When you say seeing things, I don’t know. I don’t want to say yes to something and then make it sound bigger than it is. I haven’t noticed, like, a person standing there that disappears or anything I can clearly point to. Sometimes I’ll think I saw movement out of the corner of my eye, but I don’t know if that’s just being tired or the light or me being on edge. I don’t really count that the same way, because I can’t say for sure.

And with believing things, it’s mostly like what I told you already. I don’t have another whole example coming to mind right now. It’s hard because when I’m in it, it feels connected to everything, but sitting here trying to separate it out, I don’t know what counts and what doesn’t. So… no, not really outside of what I already described.
Have you ever felt that your thoughts are being controlled by something outside of you, or that someone is putting thoughts into your mind?

I don’t know if I’d say it like… someone putting thoughts in my head, exactly. It wasn’t like a thought dropped in and I could tell it came from outside. It was more that once I got the idea about the building people, it felt locked in. Like I was sure they had marked me, and the hallway lights and those little looks people gave each other were part of it.

Even when my supervisor showed me the camera and said, “Look, nothing is happening,” I still couldn’t let it go. I could see the screen, I could see what he was trying to show me, but in my mind it was like, well, of course it won’t show on the camera, because they know where the cameras are, or the real warning is in small things you can’t catch right. So it wasn’t exactly controlled thoughts, but it did feel like I couldn’t get away from that belief once it got in there. It felt too true at the time.
Have you ever felt that your thoughts were being inserted into your mind by someone else or that something outside of you was controlling your thoughts?

I know I kind of answered this already, but… no, not exactly like thoughts being inserted, like somebody placing them there word for word. It didn’t feel like I could point and say, “That thought came from that person,” or anything like that.

But what did happen was, once I got it in my mind that the building people had marked me, it felt so strong I couldn’t shake it. Like it was just true. My supervisor even showed me the camera, trying to prove nothing was happening, and I could look right at it and still feel sure there was something going on. I kept thinking the hallway lights meant something, and the little looks people gave each other were like warnings about me.

So I don’t know if that’s the same as something controlling my thoughts. It felt more like the belief had control of me, if that makes sense. Like even when somebody showed me evidence, my mind found a way around it and said, “No, they just know how to hide it.”
Have you ever felt that your actions, like moving your arms or legs, were being controlled by something or someone outside of yourself?

No… I don’t think I’ve had it where my arms or legs were being moved by somebody else, like a puppet or something. I can’t really say that happened.

What I keep coming back to is more the other thing I was trying to explain — like my body was mine, I was walking myself, doing my job, all that. But in my head I was still sure those building people had marked me somehow. Even after my supervisor showed me the camera and there wasn’t anything there, I still felt like, no, that doesn’t prove it. I kept thinking they were using the hallway lights, and the way people would glance at each other, like little signals or warnings about me.

So not controlled movements, no. It was more like I was acting normal on the outside, but I was moving around with that belief sitting on top of everything. Like I’d go down a hallway and see the light flicker or somebody look over, and I’d feel like I knew what it meant. But I don’t remember feeling like someone else was actually moving my arms or legs for me.
Have you ever found it hard to organize your thoughts or make sense of what you're thinking, even when you're not talking to someone else?

Yeah… yeah, that happens. That’s actually kind of what brings me here, I think. It’s not only when I’m talking to somebody, it starts in my head first. I’ll be trying to think one thing through, like about the keys, and then somehow it goes to jail, and then I’m thinking about the prayer rug, and then chess pieces, and it all feels connected to me while it’s happening.

But when I try to say it out loud, people look at me like they’re lost. They’ll say, “Slow down,” or “I don’t know what you mean,” or “How did you get from that to that?” And I get frustrated because in my mind I’m not trying to be confusing. I’m trying to explain it right, but it comes out all mixed up, like I’m carrying too many things at once and dropping them in the wrong order.

Even when I’m by myself, I’ll sit there trying to make sense of it, and it’s like the pieces keep moving around. The keys, the jail, the prayer rug, the chess pieces… I know those sound like separate things, but in the moment they don’t feel separate. Then afterward I can tell people couldn’t follow me, and honestly sometimes I can’t follow it back clean either.
Have you ever felt that things happening around you, like things on TV, the radio, or even people’s actions, were specifically directed at you or had a special meaning meant only for you?

Yeah… that’s probably the closest way to say it. Not so much TV or radio, at least that’s not the thing that sticks in my mind. It was more in the building, with people and lights and cameras and those kinds of things.

Like I said, even when my supervisor took me and showed me the camera, and there wasn’t anything on there — nothing showing what I thought was happening — I still couldn’t accept it. I was standing there looking at what he was showing me, and part of me knew he wanted me to see, “Look, nothing’s there,” but it didn’t settle it for me. It felt like, no, that just means they knew where the camera was, or they knew how to stay out of sight, or somebody had already covered it up.

And the hallway lights… I know how that sounds, but at the time it felt like they were being used for a reason. Like if a light flickered or came on at a certain time, it wasn’t just a light. It felt like a signal. And the way people would look at each other, even small looks, like somebody glancing over and then looking away — I would feel like that meant they were warning each other about me. Like they had marked me somehow, like I was known in the building in a way I wasn’t supposed to be.

So yes, things around me felt like they had a special meaning for me. Not in a good way. More like I was being pointed out without anybody saying it straight. Even if someone tried to explain it away, I’d still feel sure there was something behind it.
Do you sometimes find yourself speaking in a way that even you can’t make sense of, like your sentences don’t form clearly or you’re using words that don’t quite fit together?

Yeah… yeah, that happens. That’s part of why I’m here, really. My talking gets all mixed up, and I don’t always notice it right away while I’m saying it.

Like I’ll try to explain something, and I think I’m starting in the right place, like with the keys, but then it jumps to the jail, and then I’m talking about the prayer rug, and then somehow chess pieces come into it. In my head, when it’s happening, it feels like there’s a reason those things go together. It’s not like I’m just trying to say random things. I’m trying to explain what I mean. But then I see the other person’s face, or they stop me and say they can’t follow what I’m saying, and I realize it came out wrong.

Sometimes even I can’t get back to where I started. I’ll be halfway through saying it and think, wait, what was I trying to prove here, or what was the point? And then I get more frustrated, because if I slow down too much I feel like I’ll lose it, but if I keep going it comes out tangled. So yes, my sentences don’t always form clear. The words might be real words, but the way I put them together… people tell me it doesn’t make sense.
When you're speaking and your thoughts feel mixed up, do your sentences often lose their logical connection or become so disorganized that even you can't follow how you got from one idea to the next?

Yeah… yes, that’s what I mean. It’s not just that I talk fast or I’m nervous. It’s like the connection breaks, or it changes track before I even realize it changed.

I’ll be trying to explain something simple, or at least it feels simple to me when I start. Like I’ll start with the keys, because that’s where I think the point begins. Then somehow I’m talking about the jail, and then the prayer rug comes in, and then chess pieces, and while I’m saying it, I feel like I’m still explaining the same thing. But then I hear myself, or I see the other person looking confused, and I think… wait, how did I get over here?

People tell me they can’t follow what I’m saying. They’ll say, “You lost me,” or “What does that have to do with it?” And I get embarrassed and frustrated because I’m not trying to sound like that. In my head there’s a thread, but it gets knotted up, and when I try to pull it straight it just brings three more things with it.

Sometimes even I can’t trace it back. I’ll know the pieces — keys, jail, prayer rug, chess pieces — but I can’t always explain why one led to the next in a way somebody else can understand. That’s a big part of why I came in, because my talking gets all mixed up and it scares me when I can’t make it come out right.
Have you ever felt that the thoughts you're having are not your own or that someone is trying to communicate with you through your thoughts?

I don’t know if I’d say it like somebody putting thoughts in my head, exactly. It was more like… the thoughts I was having felt connected to what people in the building were doing, like they were sending me messages without saying them out loud.

Like with the cameras — even after my supervisor took me and showed me there was nothing on there, nothing proving what I thought was happening, I still couldn’t let go of it. I kept thinking, well, that doesn’t mean it’s not happening. It just means they knew how to stay off the camera, or they knew somebody was checking, or they had already fixed it so it wouldn’t show. And those thoughts felt real strong, like I wasn’t just wondering. I felt sure of it.

And the lights in the hallway, or when people would give each other those little looks… it felt like they were communicating about me. Like the lights were some kind of warning, or the looks meant, “He’s here,” or “Watch him,” or something like that. I can’t say I heard a thought that wasn’t mine, but it felt like they had marked me somehow, and I was picking up on what they were doing through everything around me.

So… not thoughts being placed in my head exactly. More like my thoughts were telling me there was a whole message going on, and it was meant for me. Even when someone tried to show me it wasn’t true, I still felt sure there was something behind it.
Have you ever felt that certain things in your environment, like sounds, images, or people’s actions, were sending you hidden messages or had a special meaning that only you could understand?

Yes. That’s… that’s really been one of the big things. I know it probably sounds strange when I say it out loud, but at the time it didn’t feel strange to me. It felt like I was noticing something I was supposed to notice.

At the building, I kept feeling like the people there had marked me somehow. Like they knew something about me, or they had decided something about me, and then they were using little things to signal it to each other. The hallway lights especially — if they flickered, or came on at a certain time, or if one part of the hall was lit and another part wasn’t, I’d take that as a warning. Like, “He’s coming,” or “watch him,” or “he’s over here now.” It didn’t feel like just regular lights. It felt like it meant something.

And people’s looks, too. Like if two people glanced at each other when I walked by, or got quiet, or looked away too fast, I would feel sure they were communicating about me without saying it. Not just being rude or gossiping — more like they had a system. Like I wasn’t supposed to understand it, but I could pick up on it.

Even when my supervisor showed me the camera and there wasn’t anything on there, I still didn’t believe that meant nothing was happening. I thought maybe they knew where the cameras were, or they had timed it, or they had already made sure it wouldn’t show. So even with somebody showing me proof, I still felt sure the building people were doing it, using the lights and those little looks to warn each other about me. It felt too connected to be nothing.

Have you ever felt that certain events, objects, or people’s actions were directly related to you in a way that others didn’t seem to understand, like things were happening specifically because of or toward you?

Yeah… yes, that’s exactly how it felt. Like things weren’t just happening around me, they were happening because of me, or toward me. Like the whole building had me in mind somehow.

I know I keep coming back to the same examples, but that’s because that’s where it was the strongest. The hallway lights, the way people looked at each other, the way someone would stop talking when I came around — it didn’t feel random. It felt like it was all tied to me. Like they had marked me, like I was the person they were watching or warning each other about.

And even when my supervisor tried to calm me down and showed me the camera, showed me there wasn’t anything on there, I still couldn’t accept that as proof. I remember thinking, no, that just means they knew how not to get caught on the camera. Or they already knew someone was going to check. Or they had some way of making sure it didn’t show up. So instead of the camera making me feel better, my mind kind of worked around it and still came back to the same thing: they’re doing something, and it’s about me.

The little looks were hard too. If two people glanced at each other after I walked by, I’d feel it in my chest, like, there it is, they know, they’re signaling. And the lights — if they flickered or came on in a certain part of the hall — I’d think it was a warning, like they were telling each other where I was. Other people would say, “That’s just a light,” or “They’re just looking,” but to me it felt connected. It felt like I was the center of what was happening, not in a good way, but like I had been singled out.

He pulled it up and said, “See, nobody’s doing anything, nobody’s signaling.” And I could see what he was showing me, I really could, but it didn’t settle it for me. I still felt sure there was something underneath it, like the camera just wasn’t catching the real part, or they knew where the cameras were. Even with him saying it wasn’t true, I couldn’t shake it. It still felt like the building people had me marked and were using the lights and those little looks to warn each other.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a major depressive episode, which would support a diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder (F25.9) over schizophrenia (F20.9).
doctor.question: Have there been times when you felt down, hopeless, or lost interest in things for several days in a row, to the point where it was hard to get through the day?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: On my bad days I sit on the edge of the bed after morning prayer feeling heavy and empty, like there is no point cleaning myself up or going outside.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about periods of feeling down or hopeless that made daily functioning difficult, which most directly matches depressed mood.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yes, that happens. More than I like to admit, honestly. There are days where I wake up and it’s like something is already sitting on my chest before I even stand up. I’ll do morning prayer, or try to, and then afterward I just sit on the edge of the bed for a long time.

I’m not even doing anything. Just sitting there. And I feel heavy, like my arms and legs are full of wet sand or something. Empty at the same time, if that makes sense. Heavy and empty together. I’ll look at my clothes, or think about washing up, brushing my teeth, getting myself together, and it feels like… what’s the point? Like going outside would take more out of me than I have.

It’s not just being tired from work. It’s more like I can’t find a reason to start. Cleaning myself up, stepping out the door, doing regular things—on those bad days it all feels too far away. I just sit there and the day starts passing without me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences delusions or hallucinations beyond the described experiences, which would help distinguish between schizophrenia (F20.9) and schizoaffective disorder (F25.9).
doctor.question: Have you ever experienced other things that others don’t seem to notice, like seeing things that aren’t there or believing something strongly that others say isn’t true, outside of what you’ve already described?

patient.answer:
I’m not sure there’s more than what I already said. I mean… the voice and the thing with the lights and people looking at me, that’s the main stuff I know how to explain.

When you say seeing things, I don’t know. I don’t want to say yes to something and then make it sound bigger than it is. I haven’t noticed, like, a person standing there that disappears or anything I can clearly point to. Sometimes I’ll think I saw movement out of the corner of my eye, but I don’t know if that’s just being tired or the light or me being on edge. I don’t really count that the same way, because I can’t say for sure.

And with believing things, it’s mostly like what I told you already. I don’t have another whole example coming to mind right now. It’s hard because when I’m in it, it feels connected to everything, but sitting here trying to separate it out, I don’t know what counts and what doesn’t. So… no, not really outside of what I already described.

I don’t know if I’d say it like… someone putting thoughts in my head, exactly. It wasn’t like a thought dropped in and I could tell it came from outside. Like I was sure they had marked me, and the hallway lights and those little looks people gave each other were part of it.

Even when my supervisor showed me the camera and said, “Look, nothing is happening,” I still couldn’t let it go. I could see the screen, I could see what he was trying to show me, but in my mind it was like, well, of course it won’t show on the camera, because they know where the cameras are, or the real warning is in small things you can’t catch right. So it wasn’t exactly controlled thoughts, but it did feel like I couldn’t get away from that belief once it got in there. It felt too true at the time.

patient.answer:
I know I kind of answered this already, but… no, not exactly like thoughts being inserted, like somebody placing them there word for word. It didn’t feel like I could point and say, “That thought came from that person,” or anything like that.

But what did happen was, once I got it in my mind that the building people had marked me, it felt so strong I couldn’t shake it. Like it was just true. My supervisor even showed me the camera, trying to prove nothing was happening, and I could look right at it and still feel sure there was something going on. I kept thinking the hallway lights meant something, and the little looks people gave each other were like warnings about me.

So I don’t know if that’s the same as something controlling my thoughts. It felt more like the belief had control of me, if that makes sense. Like even when somebody showed me evidence, my mind found a way around it and said, “No, they just know how to hide it.”

doctor.question: Have you ever felt that your actions, like moving your arms or legs, were being controlled by something or someone outside of yourself?

patient.answer:
No… I don’t think I’ve had it where my arms or legs were being moved by somebody else, like a puppet or something. I can’t really say that happened.

What I keep coming back to is more the other thing I was trying to explain — like my body was mine, I was walking myself, doing my job, all that. But in my head I was still sure those building people had marked me somehow. Even after my supervisor showed me the camera and there wasn’t anything there, I still felt like, no, that doesn’t prove it. I kept thinking they were using the hallway lights, and the way people would glance at each other, like little signals or warnings about me.

So not controlled movements, no. It was more like I was acting normal on the outside, but I was moving around with that belief sitting on top of everything. Like I’d go down a hallway and see the light flicker or somebody look over, and I’d feel like I knew what it meant. But I don’t remember feeling like someone else was actually moving my arms or legs for me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced disorganized thinking or speech outside of the described pressured and tangential speech, which could support a diagnosis of schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder.
doctor.question: Have you ever found it hard to organize your thoughts or make sense of what you're thinking, even when you're not talking to someone else?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Thinking_Speech
target_item.manifestation: What brings me here is my talking gets all mixed up—I try to explain about the keys, then the jail, then the prayer rug, then chess pieces, and people tell me they cannot follow what I am saying.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty organizing thoughts or making sense of thinking, which directly matches disorganized thinking.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yeah, that happens. That’s actually kind of what brings me here, I think. It’s not only when I’m talking to somebody, it starts in my head first. I’ll be trying to think one thing through, like about the keys, and then somehow it goes to jail, and then I’m thinking about the prayer rug, and then chess pieces, and it all feels connected to me while it’s happening.

But when I try to say it out loud, people look at me like they’re lost. They’ll say, “Slow down,” or “I don’t know what you mean,” or “How did you get from that to that?” And I get frustrated because in my mind I’m not trying to be confusing. I’m trying to explain it right, but it comes out all mixed up, like I’m carrying too many things at once and dropping them in the wrong order.

Even when I’m by myself, I’ll sit there trying to make sense of it, and it’s like the pieces keep moving around. The keys, the jail, the prayer rug, the chess pieces… I know those sound like separate things, but in the moment they don’t feel separate. Then afterward I can tell people couldn’t follow me, and honestly sometimes I can’t follow it back clean either.

doctor.question: Have you ever felt that things happening around you, like things on TV, the radio, or even people’s actions, were specifically directed at you or had a special meaning meant only for you?

target_item.name: Delusions

patient.answer:
Yeah… that’s probably the closest way to say it. Not so much TV or radio, at least that’s not the thing that sticks in my mind. It was more in the building, with people and lights and cameras and those kinds of things.

Like I said, even when my supervisor took me and showed me the camera, and there wasn’t anything on there — nothing showing what I thought was happening — I still couldn’t accept it. I was standing there looking at what he was showing me, and part of me knew he wanted me to see, “Look, nothing’s there,” but it didn’t settle it for me. It felt like, no, that just means they knew where the camera was, or they knew how to stay out of sight, or somebody had already covered it up.

And the hallway lights… I know how that sounds, but at the time it felt like they were being used for a reason. Like if a light flickered or came on at a certain time, it wasn’t just a light. It felt like a signal. And the way people would look at each other, even small looks, like somebody glancing over and then looking away — I would feel like that meant they were warning each other about me. Like they had marked me somehow, like I was known in the building in a way I wasn’t supposed to be.

So yes, things around me felt like they had a special meaning for me. Not in a good way. More like I was being pointed out without anybody saying it straight. Even if someone tried to explain it away, I’d still feel sure there was something behind it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences disorganized thinking or speech outside of the described pressured speech and thought insertion, which could further support schizophrenia over schizoaffective disorder.
doctor.question: Do you sometimes find yourself speaking in a way that even you can’t make sense of, like your sentences don’t form clearly or you’re using words that don’t quite fit together?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Thinking_Speech
target_item.manifestation: What brings me here is my talking gets all mixed up—I try to explain about the keys, then the jail, then the prayer rug, then chess pieces, and people tell me they cannot follow what I am saying.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question is directly about speech that is hard to make sense of, unclear sentences, and words not fitting together, which matches disorganized thinking and speech.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yeah, that happens. That’s part of why I’m here, really. My talking gets all mixed up, and I don’t always notice it right away while I’m saying it.

Like I’ll try to explain something, and I think I’m starting in the right place, like with the keys, but then it jumps to the jail, and then I’m talking about the prayer rug, and then somehow chess pieces come into it. In my head, when it’s happening, it feels like there’s a reason those things go together. It’s not like I’m just trying to say random things. I’m trying to explain what I mean. But then I see the other person’s face, or they stop me and say they can’t follow what I’m saying, and I realize it came out wrong.

Sometimes even I can’t get back to where I started. I’ll be halfway through saying it and think, wait, what was I trying to prove here, or what was the point? And then I get more frustrated, because if I slow down too much I feel like I’ll lose it, but if I keep going it comes out tangled. So yes, my sentences don’t always form clear. The words might be real words, but the way I put them together… people tell me it doesn’t make sense.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a formal thought disorder characterized by disorganized speech (e.g., frequent derailment or incoherence), which is a key feature of schizophrenia (F20.9) and may help distinguish it from schizoaffective disorder (F25.9), especially when mood symptoms are also present.
doctor.question: When you're speaking and your thoughts feel mixed up, do your sentences often lose their logical connection or become so disorganized that even you can't follow how you got from one idea to the next?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Thinking_Speech
target_item.manifestation: What brings me here is my talking gets all mixed up—I try to explain about the keys, then the jail, then the prayer rug, then chess pieces, and people tell me they cannot follow what I am saying.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the patient's speech and thoughts lose logical connection and become hard to follow, which directly matches disorganized thinking and speech.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yes, that’s what I mean. It’s not just that I talk fast or I’m nervous. It’s like the connection breaks, or it changes track before I even realize it changed.

I’ll be trying to explain something simple, or at least it feels simple to me when I start. Like I’ll start with the keys, because that’s where I think the point begins. Then somehow I’m talking about the jail, and then the prayer rug comes in, and then chess pieces, and while I’m saying it, I feel like I’m still explaining the same thing. But then I hear myself, or I see the other person looking confused, and I think… wait, how did I get over here?

People tell me they can’t follow what I’m saying. They’ll say, “You lost me,” or “What does that have to do with it?” And I get embarrassed and frustrated because I’m not trying to sound like that. In my head there’s a thread, but it gets knotted up, and when I try to pull it straight it just brings three more things with it.

Sometimes even I can’t trace it back. I’ll know the pieces — keys, jail, prayer rug, chess pieces — but I can’t always explain why one led to the next in a way somebody else can understand. That’s a big part of why I came in, because my talking gets all mixed up and it scares me when I can’t make it come out right.

doctor.question: Have you ever felt that the thoughts you're having are not your own or that someone is trying to communicate with you through your thoughts?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: Even when my supervisor showed me nothing was on the camera, I still felt sure the building people had marked me and were using the hallway lights and little looks to warn each other about me.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about unusual fixed beliefs involving thoughts not being one's own or communication through thoughts, which falls under delusional experiences.

patient.answer:
I don’t know if I’d say it like somebody putting thoughts in my head, exactly. It was more like… the thoughts I was having felt connected to what people in the building were doing, like they were sending me messages without saying them out loud.

Like with the cameras — even after my supervisor took me and showed me there was nothing on there, nothing proving what I thought was happening, I still couldn’t let go of it. I kept thinking, well, that doesn’t mean it’s not happening. It just means they knew how to stay off the camera, or they knew somebody was checking, or they had already fixed it so it wouldn’t show. And those thoughts felt real strong, like I wasn’t just wondering. I felt sure of it.

And the lights in the hallway, or when people would give each other those little looks… it felt like they were communicating about me. Like the lights were some kind of warning, or the looks meant, “He’s here,” or “Watch him,” or something like that. I can’t say I heard a thought that wasn’t mine, but it felt like they had marked me somehow, and I was picking up on what they were doing through everything around me.

So… not thoughts being placed in my head exactly. More like my thoughts were telling me there was a whole message going on, and it was meant for me. Even when someone tried to show me it wasn’t true, I still felt sure there was something behind it.

doctor.question: Have you ever felt that certain things in your environment, like sounds, images, or people’s actions, were sending you hidden messages or had a special meaning that only you could understand?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: Even when my supervisor showed me nothing was on the camera, I still felt sure the building people had marked me and were using the hallway lights and little looks to warn each other about me.
target_item.reason: The question is directly asking about believing environmental cues or people’s actions carry hidden special messages, which matches the delusional belief that hallway lights and people’s looks were warnings or signals about me.

patient.answer:
Yes. That’s… that’s really been one of the big things. I know it probably sounds strange when I say it out loud, but at the time it didn’t feel strange to me. It felt like I was noticing something I was supposed to notice.

At the building, I kept feeling like the people there had marked me somehow. Like they knew something about me, or they had decided something about me, and then they were using little things to signal it to each other. The hallway lights especially — if they flickered, or came on at a certain time, or if one part of the hall was lit and another part wasn’t, I’d take that as a warning. Like, “He’s coming,” or “watch him,” or “he’s over here now.” It didn’t feel like just regular lights. It felt like it meant something.

And people’s looks, too. Like if two people glanced at each other when I walked by, or got quiet, or looked away too fast, I would feel sure they were communicating about me without saying it. Not just being rude or gossiping — more like they had a system. Like I wasn’t supposed to understand it, but I could pick up on it.

Even when my supervisor showed me the camera and there wasn’t anything on there, I still didn’t believe that meant nothing was happening. I thought maybe they knew where the cameras were, or they had timed it, or they had already made sure it wouldn’t show. So even with somebody showing me proof, I still felt sure the building people were doing it, using the lights and those little looks to warn each other about me. It felt too connected to be nothing.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences delusions of reference or thought insertion, which would help distinguish between schizophrenia (F20.9) and schizoaffective disorder (F25.9).
doctor.question: Have you ever felt that certain events, objects, or people’s actions were directly related to you in a way that others didn’t seem to understand, like things were happening specifically because of or toward you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: Even when my supervisor showed me nothing was on the camera, I still felt sure the building people had marked me and were using the hallway lights and little looks to warn each other about me.
target_item.reason: The question asks about beliefs that events, objects, or people's actions have a special personal meaning or are directed toward me, which fits delusional beliefs of reference/persecution.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yes, that’s exactly how it felt. Like things weren’t just happening around me, they were happening because of me, or toward me. Like the whole building had me in mind somehow.

I know I keep coming back to the same examples, but that’s because that’s where it was the strongest. The hallway lights, the way people looked at each other, the way someone would stop talking when I came around — it didn’t feel random. It felt like it was all tied to me. Like they had marked me, like I was the person they were watching or warning each other about.

And even when my supervisor tried to calm me down and showed me the camera, showed me there wasn’t anything on there, I still couldn’t accept that as proof. I remember thinking, no, that just means they knew how not to get caught on the camera. Or they already knew someone was going to check. Or they had some way of making sure it didn’t show up. So instead of the camera making me feel better, my mind kind of worked around it and still came back to the same thing: they’re doing something, and it’s about me.

The little looks were hard too. If two people glanced at each other after I walked by, I’d feel it in my chest, like, there it is, they know, they’re signaling. And the lights — if they flickered or came on in a certain part of the hall — I’d think it was a warning, like they were telling each other where I was. Other people would say, “That’s just a light,” or “They’re just looking,” but to me it felt connected. It felt like I was the center of what was happening, not in a good way, but like I had been singled out.
